title: Which scheduler behaves like that?

prereqs.why: Each pairing is a scheduling policy and the behaviour that falls out of it.

statement:
Five scheduling policies, and the behaviour each one is known for. Pair them up.

One of the descriptions on the right belongs to none of them — it is there because it describes something people often assume a scheduler does.
hints: Two of these need information about the future that a real scheduler does not have. Only one of them is on the left.
Ask of each policy: what does it optimise, and what does it therefore give up? Every scheduler trades turnaround time against response time.
The leftover description is of a policy with no aging and no preemption by time — which is a real thing, just not one of these five.

left: Round robin with a fixed time slice
right: Optimal average turnaround time, but it has to know how long each job will run before it starts
Gives every runnable task a share of the CPU proportional to its weight, tracked by accumulated virtual runtime
A short job arriving behind a long one waits for the whole long one — the convoy effect
Bounded response time for every task, at the cost of more context switches and worse throughput
Infers which tasks are interactive by demoting those that use a whole slice and favouring those that block early
Runs the highest-priority runnable task until it blocks, and never adjusts a priority afterwards
